Cornstarch Goo

How can one bowl of goo swallow a slow mitten but stop a fast tap?

Where shall we look?

01Why does a fast smack stop at the top?↗02What happens to the grains when you push fast?↗03Why does squeezed goo look dry?↗04Why does wet sand go pale around a foot?↗

Why does a fast smack stop at the top?

Compare the deep, sunk spoon with the dull dent in the other bowl.

A little explanation & something to try

Most liquids, like water, stay just as runny however fast you push. Isaac Newton described that rule, so this goo is called non-Newtonian. A slow push lets it flow. A fast smack makes it act like a solid for a moment.

Try this. Mix about 2 scoops of cornstarch with 1 scoop of water. Rest a spoon on top, then tap the goo fast with another. Which one sinks?

What happens to the grains when you push fast?

Find the grains floating apart and the grains crowded into chains.

A little explanation & something to try

Each cornstarch grain is so tiny that about five fit across one hair. Water sits between them like a slippery layer. A slow push lets the water slip aside. A fast push shoves the grains together before the water can move, so they lock up. Scientists call this jamming.

Try this. Drag a spoon slowly through the goo, then quickly. Feel how much harder your arm has to work.

Why does squeezed goo look dry?

Look at the dull, cracked skin of the ball and the shiny puddle beside it.

A little explanation & something to try

Jammed grains need a little more room, so they poke up through the water at the surface. The skin turns dull and cracks. Stop squeezing, and the water covers them again, so the goo shines and melts.

Try this. Roll a lump of goo between your palms, then stop and open your hands. Watch it melt and drip.

Why does wet sand go pale around a foot?

Find the pale ring around the press mark in the wet sand.

A little explanation & something to try

A step pushes the sand grains a little apart. Water sinks into the new gaps, so the top looks dry for a moment. Osborne Reynolds explained this in 1885 and named it dilatancy. Cornstarch goo does a quick version of the same trick.

Try this. Next time you are at a beach, step on firm wet sand. Watch the pale ring appear, then lift your foot.

Next: Reading →

One goo, two ways

Cornstarch Goo

Soft, then hard

Little Wonderer stirs white powder into a bowl of water. The goo looks runny, like milk. A slow mitten sinks right in. Then the little one taps it fast. Tap! Now it feels as hard as a table. Big Wonderer leans in to look. How can one bowl be soft and hard?

What happens when the little one taps the goo fast?

Slow sinks, fast stops

Try two spoons. Rest one spoon on the goo and wait. It sinks slowly to the bottom. Now smack the goo with the other spoon. It stops at the top and leaves a dull dent! Most liquids act the same, fast or slow. Water does, and so does honey. This goo breaks that rule, so it is called non-Newtonian.

How is the goo different from water?

Grains in a crowd

Cornstarch is made of tiny grains. About five could sit across one hair. In the goo, thin water sits between them. Push slowly, and the water slips aside. The grains slide past like skaters. Push fast, and the water cannot move in time. The grains crash together and lock into chains. That is called jamming.

Why do the grains jam when you push fast?

Dry, then shiny

Here is a clue. Squeeze a ball of goo, and its skin turns dull and cracked. It looks almost dry! Jammed grains need a little more room, so they poke up through the water. Stop squeezing, and the grains settle back. The water covers them again, and the ball melts into a shiny puddle.

Why does the squeezed ball look dry?

A slow ribbon

Back at the table, Big Wonderer lifts a spoonful. A slow ribbon drips back into the bowl. Little Wonderer reaches up to it. Now the guess changes. The goo is not two things. It is one crowd of grains in water. Gentle pushes let them slide. Quick pushes jam them, and then the jam melts away.

How does the guess about the goo change?

Pale sand by the sea

Wet sand at the beach plays a cousin of this trick. Step on firm, wet sand, and it turns pale around your foot. Your step pushes the grains apart, so water sinks into the new gaps. Osborne Reynolds explained it in 1885. People have even run across a pool of goo. If they stop, they sink. How long can a jam last?

Why does wet sand turn pale around a foot?

Quiz

1. What happens if you tap the goo fast?

2. What is cornstarch goo made of?

3. Why does squeezed goo look dry?

4. What does wet sand do when you step on it?

Answer key
Quiz 1
A fast tap jams the grains, so the goo feels hard for a moment.
Quiz 2
It is tiny cornstarch grains with thin water between them.
Quiz 3
Jammed grains need more room, so they poke up through the water.
Quiz 4
The grains spread apart and water sinks in, so the top looks dry.

For grown-ups · Age 8

Cornstarch goo is for touching, not tasting. Cover the table and wipe spills while wet. Never pour goo down a sink, because it can clog the drain; let it dry and put it in the trash.

Age 8 with a stretch. Welcome spoken answers, pointing, drawing and dictation. Goo is for touching, not tasting.

About the pictures and numbers. Pictures are imagined, enlarged illustrations, not photographs or measurements. Math numbers are made up for the story.
